To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a rift-related detachment system is imaged in 3D seismic datasets for the first time, that this detachment controlled the structural development and sedimentation of the Liwan sub-basin during continental breakup, and that the locus of subsistence shifted oceanward during continental breakup, within ~16 m.y.

the Liwan Subbasin, in the northern South China Searepresents an excellent example of a rifted margin where the locus of continental break-up was located immediately inboard (i.e. onshore) of the main depocentre of synrift sediments.

the Liwan Subbasin was a rift-related, tilted-block basin, which was located immediately inboard from the locus of C. Oligocene continental breakup, and that it was filled with a breakup sequence of syn-rift and post-rift sediments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the architecture of a rifted continental crust in which syn-rift sedimentation was controlled by the development of a complex detachment system that was later reactivated during the post-rift phase.
the structural and depositional evolution of a rifted continental crust and how this is recorded in the stratigraphy.
the structural and depositional evolution of an asymmetric rifted margin, inboard of the continental breakup locus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the locus of subsurface deformation, and hence the locus of subsiding crust, is the key control on sedimentation and the development of rift-related structures.

the locus of continental break-up in the South China Sea is not the site where crust was thinned most significantly during the syn-rift phase of the margin’s development, but the locus of subsurface deformation that occurred in a narrow time interval (i.e. ~16 m.y.) immediately prior to continental break-up, which was followed by a rapid and significant change in the locus of crustal thinning.
rift-related detachments, which are ubiquitous on rifted margins, are the key to understanding the structural evolution and sedimentary architecture of rifted continental margins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the locus of continental stretching is not fixed, but migrates toward the ocean during the late stages of continental rifting.

the South China Sea is an excellent example of a passive continental margin that is characterized by a highly complex structural style, with multiple tilted blocks that are offset at the base by a detachment fault system.

rift-related fault systems, such as the detachment fault system imaged in this work, are likely to control the structural evolution of the entire margin, from the rifted continental crust to the oceanic crust, at least for the first ~20 million years of margin development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the locus of continental stretching and subsidence is not fixed, but rather migrates oceanward during continental breakup.

the locus of breakup is a critical control on the distribution of syn-rift and early post-rift stratal architecture on the margin, and that the location of the locus of breakup can be identified from the geometry of tilted blocks and the distribution of synrift strata.

the locus of continental stretching, and thus of continental breakup, is likely to be located within a region of complex, multi-layered faulting and that the locus of subsistence may migrate oceanward during the early stages of continental breakup.
